19761-a-girl-in-ten-thousand:
A Girl in Ten Thousand is a story for girls by L. T. Meade, a prolific writer for young readers. Its heroine is dark-eyed and sweet-faced, though her words can sound hard. She might be any age between seventeen and twenty. Meade's girls usually face school, work, or family trials. One in ten thousand is the praise her worth must earn.

Meade wrote hundreds of books for girls in her lifetime. Her stories mixed school life with moral tests and romance. Readers followed heroines who worked, studied, and held their ground. This novel fits that popular pattern. It shows what Victorian and Edwardian girls were offered as models. The charm is period charm, preserved whole.
19799-the-rural-motor-express-to-conserv:
The Rural Motor Express was a wartime plan to move farm goods by truck. Its stated aims were to conserve foodstuffs and labor and help win the war. The argument runs on efficiency: highways must be used to the maximum. Motor trucks can run where no fixed rail lines exist. They can also relieve railroads of short-haul loads. Trucks would act as feeder lines in thinly served districts.

Food rotted when rail cars ran short in wartime. A truck route from farm to town saved both crop and car space. Federal and state groups pushed the express idea in 1918. This pamphlet is their sales pitch and manual. It marks the moment trucks joined national transport planning.
19806-everyman-s-land:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote Everyman's Land as a postwar travel romance. Its speaker confesses to wanting hatred and misunderstanding. He disguised himself as a Leprechaun and sulked, he admits. It did not work with the one person who understood him. She taught him people are much the same all over the world. The voice is whimsical, wounded, and confessional at once.

The Williamsons wrote bestselling travel novels between the wars. Everyman's Land crosses Europe's battle-scarred lands. A fairy-tale mask lets the narrator say hard things lightly. The lesson he learns is the book's thesis. Travel here heals a man the war left bitter. It is a gentle, strange period piece.
19822-with-the-british-army-in-the-holy-:
Henry Charles Woods wrote With the British Army in the Holy Land about the Palestine campaign. He opens with the land's long war history. Palestine was the cock-pit of the known world before Belgium held that name. Egyptians, Assyrians, Israelites, Canaanites, Greeks, and Romans fought there. Saracens and Crusaders followed on the same high road. The British Army of 1917 marched into that deep past.

Allenby's campaign took Jerusalem and broke Ottoman rule in Palestine. Campaign histories appeared while memory was fresh. Woods writes for readers who followed the war in newspapers. Sacred geography and modern logistics fill the same chapters. The book is a primary record of that campaign. It also shows Britain framing conquest as history.
19928-sunset-pass-or-running-the-gauntle:
Sunset Pass promises a run through the gauntlet of Apache land. A captain in its pages thinks first of the children. Renegades from the reservation are out in great numbers, he says. They are supposed to be down in the Tonto Basin. Yet their moccasin tracks have shown up nearby. Charles Seltzer wrote such Arizona westerns with a working cowboy's knowledge. Fear rides every mile of this one.

The Tonto Basin was real Apache country, steep and ambush-ready. Seltzer's novels pit settlers and soldiers against that terrain. Tracks in dust carry more dread than gunfire here. Sunset Pass belongs to his early, lean westerns. It shows the genre before Hollywood standardized it. Local detail is its claim on readers.
19966-the-statesmen-snowbound:
The Statesmen Snowbound is a comic tale of congressmen trapped by weather. Its narrator pleads the sacrifices congressmen make to serve the nation. They give up home life, business interests, and personal comforts, he says. Yet unthinking persons begrudge them a little pleasure. Snow gives the statesmen that pleasure by force. Robert Grant, a Boston judge and novelist, wrote the satire. Washington marooned makes his whole joke.

Grant first published the tale in the 1880s, and it stayed famous. Snowbound politicians must amuse themselves without constituents or press. Their stranded leisure exposes pomposity and boredom alike. The piece is gentle Thackeray-style satire, American style. It also preserves Gilded Age political manners. Few Washington comedies have lasted as well.
20043-the-angel-children-or-stories-from:
The Angel Children, or Stories from Cloud-Land, tells tales for young readers about child life and loss. One girl, Genevieve, has a large playroom full of fine toys. Other children think she must be perfectly happy with so much. Yet she would trade it all for a little brother of her own.

Genevieve longs to walk in the garden with a brother and watch over him. Her mother watches her in just that caring way. The tales blend home life, faith, and gentle moral lessons. They show what children's books of the era taught about love and want.
20057-pocket-island-a-story-of-country-l:
Charles Clark Munn published Pocket Island in 1901, a story of country life in New England. The sample turns to the Maine coast and the rum trade. Rum was cheap in Nova Scotia and dear in Maine. That gap made smuggling liquor a risky but rich trade.

Munn knew Maine life well and set much of his work there. Inside, coast folk, traders, and law men move around hidden cargo. The tale mixes local color with crime and cash. Readers get a sharp look at a coast where work and smuggling often sat side by side.
20068-sarah-s-school-friend:
May Baldwin wrote Sarah's School Friend, a girls' school story set in a London home. Mrs. Clay speaks in a strong cockney voice, with dropped h sounds. She scolds Sarah, a girl of sixteen, for sharp talk at home. Sarah has called her mother a humbug and slighted her father.

That clash opens a tale of school, family, and a young girl's pride. Baldwin wrote many such books for girls of her day. Inside, friendship tests Sarah's temper and her sense of right. Readers get period speech, home friction, and the pull of a school friend's sway.
20226-snow-bound:
Snow-Bound gathers writing shaped by winter, storm, and the fireside. Its opening verse comes from Emerson on the arrival of snow. Announced by all the trumpets of the sky, the snow arrives. It seems nowhere to alight as it drives over the fields.

The whited air hides hills, woods, river, and heaven from sight. Sled and traveler stop, and housemates sit by the radiant fire. Such scenes made snowbound tales a loved winter form in New England. Readers get poems and prose that turn deep winter into warm company.
20288-edward-the-second:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Edward the Second, a history play of a weak king's fall. Edward asks why the Lord of Coventry hurries so fast past him. The bishop replies that he goes to mark the old king's funeral. But wicked Gaveston has returned, the bishop protests in alarm.

Edward vows that Gaveston shall live to be revenged on the priest. Gaveston was the king's favorite, and his exile had been forced by barons. Marlowe turns their bond into a tragedy of power, pride, and revolt. Readers get one of the great early English history plays in verse.
20311-the-bobbsey-twins-on-blueberry-isl:
Laura Lee Hope published The Bobbsey Twins on Blueberry Island in 1917. Bert sits beside his sister Flossie in a boat on Lake Metoka. He says he is hungry yet, despite having eaten not long before. He wants some of Dinah's pie, but he also wants to stay out longer.

That small choice sets the twins' holiday mood of fun and appetite. Blueberry Island gives the four Bobbsey children a camp to explore. The series blends twins, lakes, and gentle mysteries for young readers. Readers get sunny days, boat rides, and pie worth rowing home for.
20467-handbook-of-the-trees-of-new-engla:
Lorin L. Dame's Handbook of the Trees of New England is a field guide to the region's native and planted trees. It covers New England, with notes on ranges across the United States and Canada. Keys and descriptions help readers name a tree in any season.

Dame warns that near the limit of a species, size and habit change a great deal. In trees this change is often very noticeable. He also notes there is no fixed, absolute line between trees and shrubs. Such cautions make the handbook a careful tool, built for people who would test every name outdoors.
20522-the-story-of-the-mind:
The Story of the Mind is a popular survey of psychology, the science of how minds work. Its author thanks the magazines that first printed parts of it. Passages came from the Popular Science Monthly, the Century Magazine, and the Inland Educator.

The Macmillan Company and the owners of copyright also gave their leave. That list shows how the book was built: short, clear chapters first tested on magazine readers. It covers memory, feeling, instinct, and thought for people with no training. Books like this one carried the young science of psychology into ordinary homes.
20588-the-wonder-island-boys-exploring-t:
Roger T. Finlay's The Wonder Island Boys: Exploring the Island, published in 1914, continues his series about boys cast away on a strange island. The boys explore with a friendly professor's help, and every chapter teaches real skills along with the adventure. Their finds raise as many questions as they settle.

The contents promise an arrow found in the skull of an animal, and notes on different kinds of arrows. There is a light across the river, the test of firing a gun, and the disappearance of the light. The boys also learn the qualifications in scouting. Curiosity drives every chapter.
20625-young-americans-abroad-vacation-in:
Young Americans Abroad records a vacation in Europe by a party of American youths, told in letters home. The travels run through England, France, Switzerland, and Italy. Letter writing was the natural form for travel books aimed at young readers of the time.

I have just arrived at this place, one letter begins, and have found my companions on hand. All are ready for the start of the long-hoped-for voyage. The writer regrets the duties that keep their friend at home, and says all feel sorry for the absence. The letters mix sights, history, and boyish fun.
20712-trail-s-end:
G. W. Ogden's Trail's End is a Western novel of the Kansas plains after the cattle years. Its opening paints the prairie as a graveyard of hopes. Bones lie everywhere: a waste of bones, a sepulcher that does not hide its bones but spreads them to bleach under the stern sun.

They are bones of deserted houses, the skeletons of men's hopes, crumbling on sterile wastes. Into that emptied country Ogden brings his riders and ranchers, men and women chasing a second chance. Ogden knew Kansas newspaper life, and his West is drier and harder than the dime novel kind.
20885-the-promised-land:
A little girl's world once split in two: Polotzk, where she lived, and a strange land called Russia. Mary Antin opens The Promised Land with that child's sharp map. Russia was where one's father went on business, far and dim.

Antin tells how her Jewish family left Polotzk for Boston and a new life. School, English, and hard work remake her across the book's famed arc. Her memoir became a classic tale of the immigrant's road in America. Few books state the hope and cost of that change with her clarity, pride, and eye for telling detail.
20897-a-short-history-of-england:
Britain is less an island than a maze of peninsulas, says G. K. Chesterton. Sea in the fields and fields in the sea strike the eye at every turn. A Short History of England opens with that edgy, bright paradox.

Chesterton retells England's tale as a story of the common folk. Romans, Normans, kings, and revolts pass in his brisk, witty prose. He skips dry lists to chase the spirit of each age. First issued in wartime 1917, the book still charms readers who want history with a pulse, told by a master of the telling phrase.
21003-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Thanks to the Rev. Perkins and the Photochrom Company open W. D. Sweeting's Ely Cathedral guide. Their photos ground the plates that walk readers through the great church. Loans of rare, out-of-print books aided his history of the monastery and see.

Bell's Cathedrals paired sound text with fine photos for church lovers. Ely's nave, lantern, and lady chapel star in Sweeting's calm account. He sorts tangled building tales into clear, dated order. The book served as pocket guide and home study alike, a trusted mate for one of England's grandest churches.
21069-for-treasure-bound:
A November gale at Weymouth opens Harry Collingwood's treasure novel, told by a young hero who shares the author's pen name. His father never came back from a voyage and is presumed lost at sea. Hints point to a treasure island somewhere in the Pacific.

A beautiful, fast cutter is built for the search, and Collingwood writes the shipyard scenes with a working shipwright's eye. The party sails for the Pacific and meets adventures on the way. A charming young woman joins the voyage, and the hero falls in love. Treasure, family loss, and sea travel drive the tale.
21085-the-wreck-of-the-nancy-bell-or-cas:
John Conroy Hutcheson's Nancy Bell sails from Britain for New Zealand in good order, then meets a storm that leaves her rudderless and mastless. Among the passengers travels a former Royal Navy commander in disguise. He offers the captain advice, which is brushed aside as a landsman's talk.

A mutiny breaks out before the ship is wrecked off Kerguelen Island in the far southern ocean. The survivors land, build shelter, and face a hard winter there. Hutcheson gives his Jamaican, Irish, American, and Norwegian characters their own speech. The castaways must also deal with the mutineers who landed apart from them.
21132-frank-oldfield-lost-and-found:
Langhurst, a mining village in south Lancashire, opens the Reverend T. P. Wilson's temperance novel, published in London in 1872. A collier with his Davy lamp meets Alice, a woman whose looks have been scorched away by drink, searching for her boy Sammul. Drink and the pit rule the village's hard life.

Wilson wrote for the Band of Hope movement, which taught children never to start drinking. Frank Oldfield's story of being lost and found plays out among colliers, drinkers, and those trying to save them. The novel won wide circulation as a prize temperance tale, mixing dialect speech with a clear moral purpose.
21198-anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sc:
S. Spooner was a doctor who also wrote a biographical history of the fine arts. He packed this second volume of anecdotes with lives and curiosities of art. It opens with Titian: his manners, works, imitators, and his dealings with Emperor Charles V and Philip II. A sketch of Horace Vernet follows.

Later pieces range over the Colosseum, the remains of Nineveh, a palace dug up at Nimroud, and the ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum. The origin of the arch, ancient fresco and mosaic, and the Portland Vase all get entries. Published in New York, the volume serves as a lively miscellany for art lovers.
21245-three-boys-in-the-wild-north-land:
Mr Ross welcomes three sunburnt boys to Sagasta-weekee, his house full of sunshine on the Nelson River, in Egerton Ryerson Young's tale. Frank, Alec, and Sam have sailed by the Prince Arthur to York Factory on Hudson Bay. Ross, a retired Hudson's Bay Company officer, hosts them in his hunting lodge.

The boys spend a season of adventures in the wild north land. They meet Inuit travellers and learn the country from a man whose father also served the Company. Young had worked as a missionary in the region and wrote from experience. Hunting, travel, and winter coming on give the three visitors their education in the North.
21246-winter-adventures-of-three-boys-in:
A November storm rages outside while Frank, Alec, and Sam sit at breakfast in a cosy northern home in Egerton R. Young's sequel. The three boys came from Britain the previous summer by Hudson's Bay Company ship and stayed on as guests of Mr Ross. Now winter, their first in the great lone land, is the adventure.

Dog teams, whips, and the dog keeper Kinesasis start the season's lessons. Ross had spent his career in the fur trade on friendly terms with the Indigenous peoples around him, and his household keeps that closeness. Snow travel, hunting, and the long dark shape a winter the boys will not forget.
21284-six-years-in-the-prisons-of-englan:
An unnamed merchant tells how he began business in a northern city in 1856. He paid his creditors in full after a failed partnership, and still ended in prison. Frank Henderson edited the account, first printed in Temple Bar Magazine and reissued in London in 1869. The author writes for a kind brother who cheered his darkest hours.

Chapters follow his feelings on entering prison, his trial and sentence, three months in a Scottish prison, and removal to a Yorkshire one. Fellow prisoners fill the pages: an old jail bird, a soldier, an innocent convict, and a cracksman planning murder and escape. Victorian prison life is shown from a cell.
21321-before-the-dawn-a-story-of-the-fal:
Joseph A. Altsheler set this 1903 novel in Richmond as the Confederacy falls. It opens on a raw, gusty morning. A thin, brown-faced officer with a stiff left arm and a bullet-holed uniform boards a train for the capital. Chapters move through the Mosaic Club, the Secretary's manoeuvres, and a woman in brown pursued through the city.

Robert and Lucia carry the love story through the pall of winter, while the chapters on feeding the hungry show a starving capital. Altsheler knew the Civil War deeply and wrote many novels of it. The fall of Richmond ends an era for his characters, in flight, fire, and change of flags.
21357-nic-revel-a-white-slave-s-adventur:
Nic Revel grows up on a small Devon estate where poachers keep raiding the family's salmon pool. In George Manville Fenn's tale, a big fight at the pool ends with Royal Navy men supporting the Revels. Wounded in the dark, Nic is mistaken for a poacher and press-ganged with the men he fought.

Carried to America still half conscious, he is sold by the ship to a slave dealer. The dealer sells him on to a settler far up a river in alligator land. Hard work and poor food follow for Nic and a poacher turned friend. Their long effort to escape and reach Devon again drives the tale's second half.
21391-great-african-travellers-from-mung:
Finding the sources of great rivers drove the men in W. H. G. Kingston's Great African Travellers. The book runs from Mungo Park to Livingstone and Stanley, the best known names in African travel. At the start of their age, the coasts were mapped, but the deep interior was not.

Kingston tells how each traveller set out from a coastal base and won leave to pass inland. Some African rulers gave a warm welcome, and others did not. The Nile and its twin branches drew many of the boldest trips. The book gives a clear, joined account of a whole age of bold travel.
21393-hendricks-the-hunter-or-the-border:
Hendricks earns his living by the gun in W. H. G. Kingston's tale of Zululand, Hendricks the Hunter. He hunts game and trades skins and other goods along the border farms. The book opens among the steep ranges and deep valleys of South Africa.

One long hunting trip carries the action, told with Kingston's usual care for place. Wild beasts, snakes, and thirst are constant threats on the trail. The Zulu people he meets are drawn with warmth when they prove friends. A heavy wagon, built of stink wood, hauls the loads. The tale mixes trade, travel, and danger in equal parts.
21416-randy-of-the-river-or-the-adventur:
Randy Thompson works his way up from the river bank in Horatio Alger's Randy of the River, published in 1906. Randy is a patient fisher who waits at the hole while other boys wander off. That same steady grit marks all his dealings in the tale.

As a young deckhand on a river boat, Randy meets greed, blame, and unfair charges. In one key scene he tells Mr Polk that a loss was not his fault, and he will not stand for it. Alger's hero holds to honest work and a clear name. The tale rewards him in the usual Alger way, by steady rise.
21458-charley-laurel-a-story-of-adventur:
Charley Laurel passes into a sailor's hands as a small child in W. H. G. Kingston's Charley Laurel. At a West Indian place just attacked by the British, his nurse is fatally wounded. Seaman Dick Driver takes the boy and raises him aboard ship.

Their luck runs wild: cast away on a raft, picked up by pirates, saved by a privateer. On a South Pacific island, captors hold the two apart. Charley's trick frees Dick, and a British ship takes them off. In England a shipowner's family takes to the boy and sends him to school.
21489-the-secret-of-the-island:
W. H. G. Kingston translated Jules Verne's The Secret of the Island from the French. The tale follows a party cast away on a Pacific island after a balloon trip. Kingston also gave English readers a version of The Swiss Family Robinson.

Pirates and escaped convicts from Australia trouble the settlers' hard-won home. At odd times, unseen help saves them, as if some power watched over the island. That power proves to be Captain Nemo, hidden in a vast cave with his wealth. The book stands as a sequel to Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
21579-snarleyyow-or-the-dog-fiend:
Snarleyyow, the dog fiend, survives every attempt on his life in Captain Marryat's novel of 1837. Frost coats the spars and small iron guns of his ship at dawn. All hands but his owner treat the ugly beast with spite, and he returns the favour.

Marryat sets the tale when a Dutch-born king sat on the English throne. His Dutch courtiers and officials fill the court, and the cutter runs often to the Netherlands. Side plots breed in those crossings, among a crew of hopeless, unkind folk. The dog outlasts them all, as nasty at the end as at the start.
21591-the-harbours-of-england:
John Ruskin writes on Turner's ports in The Harbours of England, given here from his complete works. Turner and the engraver Lupton began the Ports of England as a serial in 1826. Only three numbers appeared before the plan stalled for want of time.

Ruskin's text, first issued in full in 1856, treats Dover, Ramsgate, Plymouth, and Portsmouth. Margate, Falmouth, Sidmouth, Whitby, Deal, and Scarborough follow in short, rich chapters. Collectors paid eleven or twelve guineas for proof sets of the plates. The editor laments that Ruskin's readers have passed the book by, and this edition makes the case anew.
21721-the-coral-island:
Ralph Rover tells his own story in Ballantyne's most famous book, a tale of boys cast away on a South Sea island. Ralph was born at sea, the son and grandson of captains, and roving runs in his blood. He ships out as a boy, hungry for adventure in foreign lands, and a wreck gives him more than he asked for.

On the island, Ralph and his companions must find food, build shelter, and face dangers from sea and land. Ballantyne never saw the Pacific, yet his coral shores and lagoons convinced generations of readers. The book shaped nearly every island adventure written after it, and boys read it eagerly for a century.
21729-dusty-diamonds-cut-and-polished-a-:
London street children stand at the center of this Ballantyne novel, first published in 1884. Two homeless boys near Whitechapel, in the East End, are taken off the streets by rescuers. They are trained up and sent to Canada, to live with a farmer's family there. Their story runs beside a grimmer one.

The mother of one boy struggles with drink, too many children, and a violent, thieving husband. Her eldest daughter holds the family together while the father sits in jail. Ballantyne drew the title from his theme: rough lives hold worth that care can polish. The tale gives a close look at street life in the London of his day.
21732-fort-desolation-red-indians-and-fu:
Jack Robinson is the plain, quiet hero of this Ballantyne tale of a lonely fur-trade fort in Rupert's Land. To strangers he looks like the most commonplace of men, sandy-haired and unnoticed. In truth a deep stream of romance runs in him, flashing out only in rare moments. Solitude does not suit him, yet his work gives him plenty of it.

Ballantyne sets the story among the traders and native peoples of the far northern wilderness. He knew that world from his own Hudson's Bay years in Canada. Trade, travel, and the long winters of an outpost shape the tale. Jack's calm grit holds it together from first page to last.
21826-my-pet-recipes-tried-and-true-cont:
Favorite dishes of a church circle fill My Pet Recipes, a Canadian cookbook gathered by the ladies and friends of St. Andrew's Church in Quebec. Each recipe comes as a pet of its giver, tried and true in her own kitchen. The pages carry the marks of their time and place. Furs by Holt, Renfrew are advertised at the front, and grocers promise the freshest goods in Quebec.

Community cookbooks like this one preserved home cooking that no chef ever wrote down. Soups, cakes, and preserves pass from neighbor to neighbor in print. The ads around the recipes are part of the record too, showing the shops those cooks relied upon. For food historians, such books are gold: plain, practical, and close to real tables.
21948-little-busybodies-the-life-of-cric:
Insects get biographies in Little Busybodies, a nature book for children aged eight to fourteen. Jeannette Marks and Julia Moody of Mount Holyoke College published it in 1909. The life of crickets, ants, bees, beetles, and their kin is told as story-led science. A journey to Rangeley Village frames the lessons. Chapters march with the little army of grasshoppers, listen to cricket fiddlers, and ask how Katy did with the katydids.

Dragonflies go fishing, and may-flies live their brief day in the telling. The book belongs to a Harper series covering crabs, shells, fish, birds, and flowers in the same plan. Pictures name the cast, from cicada killer to mole cricket. It teaches close watching as a form of fun.
22108-the-untroubled-mind:
Herbert J. Hall, a doctor who treated nervous patients, wrote The Untroubled Mind about worry and restless living. Hall warns that peace will not arrive in a flash of revelation. Change comes slowly, by returning again and again to honest work. He refuses to belittle that struggle; he wants it fought at a better level.

His counsel joins medical sense to a quiet faith in purposeful occupation. Ordered work, outdoor life, and simple interests steady the mind in his practice. The book grew from Hall's work with invalids who had lost their trades. It is an early, humane entry in the literature of mental health, still readable for its calm good sense.
22142-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers, a Scottish minister and antiquary, edited The Modern Scottish Minstrel. Volume V continues his gathering of Scotland's songs with lives of the song-makers. The series aimed to carry Scottish song from Burns's age into Rogers's own century. Each song comes with notes on its author and its air.

This volume's opening matter praises bodies that relieved poor men of genius and learning. Such societies kept Scotland's literary spirit alive, Rogers believed. Portraits of the poets face their songs. The Minstrel volumes are quarries for anyone studying Scottish song: words, tunes, and biographies together. Volume V holds the later letters of the alphabet of poets.
22201-the-butterfly-s-funeral-a-sequel-t:
The Butterfly's Funeral continues the insect world made famous by The Butterfly's Ball. That tiny verse fable, written for the Roscoe children, had charmed Georgian England. In this sequel the butterfly is dead and must be buried in state. The corpse is embalmed at sunset and enclosed in a case spun by the silkworm herself.

The hornet helps lay the coffin on a bier of myrtle and jasmine. Beetles, bees, and all the ball's bright company form the funeral train. The poem teaches children nature's names through pageantry and grief. Such miniature books, printed for the nursery trade, were the picture books of their day, and this sequel kept a beloved trifle alive.
22210-in-the-forbidden-land:
A. Henry Savage Landor travelled in Tibet when Tibet was closed to foreigners, and In the Forbidden Land tells how. Landor was captured, tortured, and expelled by Tibetan officials in 1897. His two-volume account caused a sensation on its release. Reviewers quoted in the book praise its vivid verbal pictures and the author's own drawings and photographs.

Landor describes passes, monasteries, and the men who hunted him across the plateau. He presents himself as artist and explorer in one, emphasising the letterpress with his pencil. Some contemporaries doubted details; the adventure's core was never in question. The book remains a classic of forbidden-frontier travel writing.
22229-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Volume VI closes Charles Rogers's Modern Scottish Minstrel, his great gathering of Scotland's songs. Rogers pairs each song with the life of its maker. This volume's frontispiece shows Paisley, birthplace of Tannahill, Alexander Wilson, and John Wilson. Weaver poets and Paisley shawls stand behind many of these songs.

Rogers opens with a reflection on poetry as the first language of nations. The lyric muse, he writes, chose lands of mountain and flood, and left them when liberty died. The songs that follow, with their notes, prove his devotion to that idea. Six volumes strong, the Minstrel remains a working library of Scottish song and song-makers.
22342-supermind:
Supermind is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg, again featuring Malone. He agrees peacefully with whatever the Director of the FBI says. He eyes that powerful man with due wariness.

After all, Malone argues, the news is nothing new. The country has always been going to hell in a handbasket. One way or another, he says, decline is the old story. That shrug sets the tale's tone of dry humor under pressure. A supermind, by the title, stands behind the trouble. Readers get a wry period story where vast powers and federal men meet one unflappable talker.
22377-rollo-in-switzerland:
Rollo in Switzerland sends a young American traveler through the Alps. Rollo was the hero of a famous series of travel books for children. His last day in Paris opens this volume's journey.

In Paris, Rollo learned the passport system by actual experience. That lesson in paperwork readied him for crossing into Switzerland. The series taught geography through a boy's questions and mishaps. Adults in the books explain countries, customs, and rules as they go. Young readers toured Europe without leaving home. This Swiss volume offers mountains and manners together. It shows how nineteenth-century families taught travel, order, and curiosity in one small package.
22581-the-child-voice-in-singing-treated:
Francis E. Howard wrote The Child Voice in Singing, a teaching treatise published in 1895. Howard treats the child's singing voice from both a bodily and a practical angle, with special care for girl and boy choirs. His audience is the large body of vocal music teachers in public schools.

Howard argues that the core of all vocal teaching must be brought home to school instructors in a convincing way. He holds that teachers accept a new idea only when its truth is proved to them plainly. The book therefore mixes body science with classroom argument. It remains a useful window on how singing was taught, and how reformers tried to change school music from inside.
22590-wind:
Wind is a science fiction story with a Dutch flavor, set partly around Earth's seas and partly on Venus. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its dialogue name-checks the IJsselmeer and the old Zuider Zee, and its sailors speak like men used to rough water and tall claims.

In the sample, a captain named Heemskerk teases young Jan about returning punctually, broom at the masthead and all, the old sailor's sign of a swept, victorious sea. Jan answers that brooms are scarce on Venus. The blend of sea lore and space travel marks the tale's playful spirit. It offers readers a short, salty mix of nautical tradition and planetary adventure.
22756-the-enchanted-island:
The Enchanted Island is a children's fantasy issued by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1919. The catalog record credits the publisher. Its world is an archipelago of four big islands, each a separate kingdom that has nothing to do with the others, ripe ground for a young traveler's adventures.

The largest island is called the Island of Sunne because it is the nicest and has the finest weather. It never rains there in the daytime, but only at night, which, the narrator admits, is very convenient. That confiding voice, half guide-book and half fairy tale, carries the story from kingdom to kingdom. howards-end: E. M. Forster's 1910 Howards End: "Only connect" — the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and England's soul. The great Edwardian novel of class and culture. A masterpiece of the modern age. Forster's England in one house's fate, the novel of connection.
john-bull-s-other-island:
John Bull's Other Island is a play by Bernard Shaw about England and Ireland. It opens at Great George Street, Westminster, in the rooms of Doyle and Broadbent, civil engineers. The partners are bachelors and bosom friends who live where they work. Their sitting room smells of tobacco and holds drawing boards, plans, and tracing paper.

On the walls hang a map of South America, a portrait of Gladstone, and cartoons of Balfour and Chamberlain. The time is a summer afternoon in 1904, as the scene directions fix it. Broadbent, the English partner, arrives with luggage in the first moments. Doyle, his Irish partner, gives Shaw his pair for the argument ahead: English confidence meets Irish clear sight in business and politics.
landholding-in-england:
Joseph Fisher wrote this history of landholding in England. He signed himself a fellow of the Royal Historical Society. A proverb about tillage and judgment stands as his motto.

Fisher argues that farming is the most useful of all arts. A nation draws its food and solid wealth from the soil, he says. His history traces how English land was held across the ages. Laws, customs, and great estates all shape that story. The book suits readers curious about how land law grew in England. Fisher links land law to the daily bread of the poor. That link gives dry legal history a human stake.
letters-of-a-traveller-or-notes-of-thing:
William Cullen Bryant gathered his Letters of a Traveller from sixteen years of journeys. The letters record things seen in Europe and America. Bryant admits they form no regular account of any single tour.

Instead, he offers occasional sketches of whatever caught his attention. Most pieces had already appeared in print before this collection. Bryant, a poet and newspaper editor, writes with a traveler's calm curiosity. Scenery, towns, and customs all receive his measured attention. The book preserves an early American voice observing the wider world. Bryant helped found the New York Evening Post's voice. Travel gave his editorials a wider, calmer horizon.
letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-2-from-rom: "From Rome to the End" is the subtitle of this second volume of Franz Liszt's correspondence. It takes up where the Paris-to-Rome volume leaves off, in the composer's later years. The editor was La Mara, and Constance Bache translated the letters into English. Because the hosted sample holds nothing past the Project Gutenberg header, no contents are described here; the title page is the whole evidence.
lewis-rand:
Mary Johnston published her novel Lewis Rand in 1908. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York, with pictures by F. C. Yohn. Johnston had written To Have and to Hold and Prisoners of Hope.

She inscribed the book to Senator John Tyler Morgan's memory. Thirty years a senator, he was a good man and patriot, she writes. Her tale turns to Virginia politics in Jefferson's era. Ambition drives the hero whose name titles the book. Courtship and courtrooms, one picture caption jokes, both await him. Johnston's Virginia settings drew on deep family roots there. Aaron Burr's era shadows the politics behind her romance.
life-in-morocco-and-glimpses-beyond:
Budgett Meakin wrote this account of life in Morocco. His earlier books described the Moors and the land itself. Contents range across dress, courtesy, food, slavery, and trade. Festivals, saints, marriage, and funeral rites all receive chapters.

Meakin also treats the Berbers and the Jews of Morocco. City descriptions run from Tangier and Fez to far southern towns. Travel pieces recall journeys in Moorish guise and by bicycle. The volume offers a full, close portrait of Moroccan society. His Land of the Moors described towns from Tangier to Mogador. Reminiscences include a bicycle journey to Marrákesh and Moorish disguise.
life-of-harriet-beecher-stowe-compiled-f:
Charles Edward Stowe compiled this life of his mother from her papers. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1890. Harriet Beecher Stowe suggested the compilation herself, her son explains. Failing strength kept her from writing the recollections alone.

With her limited assistance, he built the story from letters and journals. The preface carries her own notes of instruction for readers. A handwritten letter appears among the illustrations. The result lets the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin speak largely for herself. The Riverside Press at Cambridge printed the electrotyped sheets. A Richmond portrait of Stowe fronts the compiled letters.
lonesome-land:
B. M. Bower opens this western novel with Val's arrival. Well-meant advice and a lady in a temper follow quickly. A shivaree and Cold Spring Ranch set the scene. Manley's fire guard and a prairie fire raise the stakes.

Kent rides to the rescue after desolation strikes the ranch. Val's awakening leads her toward becoming an author. A blotched brand and Kent's confession complicate the middle. Bower had written Chip, of the Flying U, before this tale. Val decides and Kent confesses before the compact chapter. Retribution closes the twenty-four chapter contents list.
maiwa-s-revenge-or-the-war-of-the-little:
Maiwa's Revenge, or The War of the Little Hand, is an Allan Quatermain tale by H. Rider Haggard. Quatermain tells it a week after his story of the Three Lions. The preface swears its strangest incident was 'plagiarized' from real life. Chief Mandara, on Africa's east coast, truly owned the 'thing that bites.'

Eight short chapters carry the tale from Gobo's blow to Maiwa avenged. A morning's sport turns into rounds of real fighting. Maiwa's message brings a plan of campaign and an attack. Wambe, her cruel husband, has wronged her past pardon. Haggard writes swift, red-blooded African adventure. The story shows Quatermain in a short, sharp war.
malayan-literature-comprising-romantic-t:
Malayan Literature gathers romantic tales, epic poetry, and royal chronicles in English. Chauncey C. Starkweather translated them, he says, for the first time. His special introduction praises the Epic of Bidasari above all. He calls it the most charming poem of Malayan letters.

Bidasari leads readers through haunted palaces and beauteous gardens. Bowmen and lancers hurry past, then djinns and spirit-princes appear. Starkweather finds imagery and luxury in the old Malay tales. Royal chronicles add kings and courts to the romance. The collection opened a rich, little-known tradition to English readers. It remains a pioneering window onto Southeast Asian letters.
marjorie-s-new-friend:
Marjorie's New Friend is a girls' novel by Carolyn Wells of Patty fame. It opens with a bothersome bag and a welcome Christmas gift. Merry Christmas and Happy New Year carry Marjorie into winter. Then comes a tearful time, with the going of Gladys.

Against that loss stands the coming of Delight, the new friend. A visit to Cinderella, a straw-ride, and making valentines follow. Marjorie is held captive in one chapter and freed in fun. Goldfish, kittens, and a pleasant school fill her days. A sea trip and a valentine party close the year. Wells writes friendship as a child's great adventure.
midwinter-certain-travellers-in-old-engl:
John Buchan published this historical novel in 1923. Its scene is England in 1745, as Bonnie Prince Charlie's rebel army marches south. Alastair Maclean, among the Prince's most loyal supporters, rides ahead on a secret mission. The publisher's description calls the book certain travellers in old England.

On the road Maclean is befriended by two extraordinary men. One is Dr. Samuel Johnson, then an aspiring man of letters. The other is the shadowy figure known only as Midwinter. Buchan blends Jacobite adventure with the talk and travel of Georgian England. The result mixes spying, loyalty, and literary portraiture.
money-island:
Andrew J. Howell Jr. copyrighted this North Carolina story collection in 1908. It was printed at Wilmington by the Commercial Printing Company. The volume holds two tales: Money Island and The Conquest of Jamesby. An illustration shows the little island among the marshes.

Money Island lies in Greenville Sound, not far from Wilmington. The story concerns buried treasure hidden there long ago. Jonathan Landstone told the tale, and wrote it down himself so it would be told correctly. Howell presents the words as Landstone's own. Local legend, a secretive island, and old Carolina families give the tales their flavor of regional history.
multatuli-walter-pieterse-a-story-of-hol:
Multatuli, the pen name of Eduard Douwes Dekker, tells a Dutch boy's growth in Walter Pieterse, here in English. Young Walter, shy and dreamy, comes of age in Amsterdam. His tender heart clashes with a stiff, narrow world of school, church, and trade.

Dekker writes with the satirical fire that made Max Havelaar famous. Here the target is Holland itself: its cant, greed, and small pieties. Walter's first loves and shames carry the author's own boyhood within them. The novel stands as a humane, rebellious classic of Dutch letters, tender toward the young and merciless toward humbug.
my-discovery-of-england:
Stephen Leacock, the Canadian humorist, lectures on his first trip to England. Sir Owen Seaman introduced his first London talk with jokes. Seaman notes Leacock teaches political economy for a living. Humor, he says, is the professor's recreation.

The book grew from those lectures, issued in 1922. Leacock views old England with a colonial's fresh eye. Customs, class, and speech all draw his gentle mockery. V1 praised the tour as sharp yet warm throughout. Leacock never sneers, and his fun cuts both ways. It remains a model of kind satire, proof that a visitor can love a place and laugh at it too.
narratives-of-shipwrecks-of-the-royal-na:
William O. S. Gilly compiled these Royal Navy wreck tales from Admiralty papers. John W. Parker issued the book in London in 1850. His father, Canon William Stephen Gilly, wrote the preface. The wrecks span the war years from 1793 to 1849.

The contents list lost ships in a grim roll call. Boyne, Amphion, Tribune, and Queen Charlotte lead the list. Apollo, Hindostan, Romney, and Venerable follow among many more. Each tale draws on official documents of the loss. Storms, reefs, fire, and war took these ships and crews. The book is a sober memorial to naval disaster in the age of sail.
nasa-tm-19640017347-adaptive-flight-cont:
Lawrence W. Taylor, Jr. and Elmor J. Adkins of NASA's Flight Research Center wrote this paper. They gave it at an AIAA specialists meeting on April 28, 1964. Their subject is adaptive flight control, weighed pro and con. Such systems adjust their own settings while in flight.

The authors say interest grew from trouble with fixed-gain controls. Fast aircraft change character so much that one setting fails. Gain scheduling had fallen from favor for three stated reasons. It needed vast flight data, took long to tune, and broke with each design change. An adaptive system would pick its best gain on its own. The paper weighs that promise for craft like the X-15.
nasa-tm-19650014317-low-speed-investigat:
William P Henderson and Alexander D Hammond at Langley studied a half-wing model that could change its sweep. The pivot sat outboard, away from the body. Their low-speed tests focused on high-lift devices and on sideways control. Leading edge and trailing edge flaps were moved to see their effect.

A swing wing must still take off and land well. At low speed, flaps do much of that work. The tests show how flap settings changed lift and lateral control for this layout. Designers of variable-sweep aircraft needed exactly that kind of data. The half-wing, or semispan, model let them test one side in detail.
nasa-tm-19660006537-saturn-s-i-10-static:
Marshall's Measuring and Evaluation Section issued this final report on January 11, 1966, with vibration and sound data from static tests of Saturn vehicle S-I-10. In a static test, the stage is held down while its engines fire. Sensors record how the vehicle shakes and how loud it becomes. Both can damage the vehicle or its payload if they run too high.

Data appear as acceleration against frequency and sound pressure level against frequency. Statistical profiles complete the record. Engineers use such profiles to set the shaking and noise levels that parts must survive. The report preserves the measured environment of a real Saturn first stage under full thrust.
nasa-tm-19660006764-significant-electron:
Members of the Echo II project staff at Goddard presented this review in San Francisco in August 1965. Project Echo flew giant balloon satellites that bounced signals between ground stations. The review gathers the project's electronic work and its experimental results in one place. Early contents cover the project's objectives and how they were carried out, in a piece by H L Eaker.

Other sections, per the catalog note, treat prototype ground spheres and a television and beacon telemetry system. Communication experiments with Echo II close the set. As a project record, it shows how much ground electronics a supposedly simple balloon satellite actually required to work.
nasa-tm-19660015346-magnetic-field-restr:
Norman F Ness at Goddard wrote rules in July 1964 for keeping stray magnetism out of two spacecraft, IMP-F and IMP-G. The IMP satellites measured magnetic fields in space. A spacecraft's own parts can fake a field and spoil those readings. Ness sets fabrication procedures to prevent that fault. His contents start with non-magnetic electronic and structural parts.

Wiring gets detailed attention, with leads dressed so their fields cancel out. Solar cell wiring and power leads receive their own guidance, as strong stray sources. Magnetic field tests follow the build rules. Every magnetometer mission since has lived by rules of this kind, first written down in documents like this one.
nasa-tm-19670008638-data-book-for-enviro:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland prepared this data book through its Test and Evaluation Division. The book serves engineers who test spacecraft against the harsh conditions of launch and space. Its preface states the purpose plainly: keep those engineers current and give them a reference that stays up to date.

The opening sections present the status of Goddard satellite programs and NASA launch vehicle and sounding rocket programs. Another section summarizes the test levels then in force for Goddard environmental testing. It also gathers a bibliography of reports on past and current test programs. The volume gathers data on the space and launch settings that spacecraft must survive.
nasa-tm-19670017954-least-squares-analys:
L. Elfenbein, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis on February 3, 1967. It applies the least squares method to tracking data from AS-202, an uncrewed Apollo test flight. The data came from the unified S-band system, which combined tracking, voice, and data links in one radio system for Apollo.

Elfenbein analyzed high-speed range rate and sideways angular data gathered by the Merritt Island and Bermuda ground stations during powered flight. The method fitted smooth polynomials to the tracking data over short time intervals, always in the least squares sense. How far the real data scattered around each fit then measured the noise in the system. The data ran at ten samples per second. The report presents station-by-station results. They give a preliminary picture of the unified S-band system's noise characteristics.
nasa-tm-19680002160-interaction-of-the-m:
Y. C. Whang, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It treats the interaction of the magnetized solar wind with the Moon. The Moon carries no global magnetic shield of its own, so the wind meets the lunar surface almost directly, unlike at Earth.

Explorer 35 had entered lunar orbit in July 1967 to study exactly this encounter. Its results indicated that no detached bow shock wave exists near the Moon. Whang therefore treats the flow theoretically as a free molecule flow of magnetized plasma, deriving the ion density and flux around the Moon. A sizable empty cavity forms just downstream, with plasma changing rapidly across its boundary. Behind the Moon stretches a long wake on the dark side, slightly deflected toward the magnetic field lines. The wake runs about one lunar diameter thick, lengthening far downstream.
nasa-tm-19680027016-applications-of-rada:
Richard F. Broderick, Richard G. Fenner, and Robert Chick, of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, presented this paper in April 1966 at a Southwestern IEEE meeting. They survey how radar serves spacecraft and spaceflight, in programs then flying and in plans still on paper. Gemini, Apollo, and Surveyor had each made radar essential, they open by noting.

Mercury craft carried only beacons that answered ground radar, while Gemini paired radar with a computer to achieve rendezvous. Surveyor used Doppler radar as a landing aid on the Moon. Apollo's lunar module was to carry both rendezvous and landing radars. Planned experiments included side-looking radar, scatterometers, and sharper altimeters and velocity sensors.
nasa-tm-19690004743-effect-of-bleed-syst:
Bobby W. Sanders and Robert W. Cubbison of Lewis Research Center tested inlet bleed systems at Mach 2.50 in this December 1968 memorandum. The axisymmetric mixed-compression inlet uses bleed to control boundary layer air. Two bleed geometries with very different total porous area were compared.

Bleed-exit areas were varied to set different back pressures. At equal supercritical bleed flow, the higher porous-area setup gave higher total-pressure recovery at critical operation. It also cut bleed drag substantially, by the share the authors report. The cost was a complete loss of subcritical stability margin. Careful bleed-exit control let engine airflow drop well below critical without an unstart.
nasa-tm-19690016855-experiences-with-ber:
William Fecych of Lewis Research Center recounts problems with beryllium in the Plum Brook Reactor in this May 1969 memorandum. Intense neutron exposure made major core components swell, distort, and fail. Beryllium parts sat in the reactor's highest neutron fluence regions, where damage ran worst.

Fecych describes the reactor's material surveillance programs in detail. He explains the failure mode of the damaged components. Replacement methods for the swollen parts are laid out step by step. Associated health hazards of handling irradiated beryllium receive attention as well. Distortion is charted against neutron fluence for future planning. The account guides operators of other research reactors facing the same swelling problem.
nasa-tm-19690023855-a-comparison-between:
William E. Shenk and Earl R. Kreins of Goddard Space Flight Center compare observed winds with satellite cloud motions in this July 1969 preprint, X-622-69-285. Their cloud motions come from the Nimbus II satellite's high resolution infrared radiometer, over ocean areas. If drifting clouds faithfully ride the wind, satellites could supply wind data where no weather stations exist.

Motions averaged over two overlapping orbits were checked against wind vectors read from pressure charts. Coastlines in both views corrected the satellite's pointing, and cloud centers fixed each cloud's position. Generally, the authors find, cloud direction stayed within twenty degrees of the wind. Cloud speed stayed within fifteen knots of it as well, a promising verdict.
nasa-tm-19700003621-accelerations-on-24-:
Carl A. Wagner wrote this November 1969 Goddard preprint on accelerations felt by twenty-four-hour satellites. Six such satellites, from Syncom and Early Bird to Intelsat craft, supply tracking records from 1963 through 1969. Sitting in step with Earth's rotation, these craft feel steady pushes from the gravity field's longitude lumps. Those pushes, read carefully, map the field itself.

Wagner reduces the records to thirty-five well determined accelerations from the uneven gravity field. From them he derives two best resonant gravity fields, carried to fourth order. He also relocates the four east-west balance points where a geostationary satellite can rest. Recent gravity models, he notes, clearly improve on the best models of 1966.
nasa-tm-19710002749-the-use-of-automatic:
NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, issued this study as document PM-64. It applies automatic control theory and a simple math model of the pilot to helicopter control design. The goal is a manual control system that helps a pilot fly a landing approach on instruments, down to a hover at touchdown.

The work began as a brief one-week investigation in July 1968. Its synthesis technique proved quite successful in that short trial. The method was later used to define flight director control laws for Langley's tandem rotor helicopter. Tests ran on a fixed-base simulator with a nonlinear model of that aircraft, switching between hover and cruise control modes.
nasa-tm-19710014299-process-and-apparatu:
J W Wasquin, Marvin Estes, and David Webb of the Marshall Space Flight Center described a new way to make diamonds in NASA TM X-64543. Their laboratory was the Product Engineering and Process Technology Laboratory. The method synthesizes diamond grit rather than gem stones. Diamond grit serves as a hard abrasive for grinding and smoothing other materials.

The abstract calls the method new and unique. The grit it makes has many crystals joined together. Its sizes match those commonly used in grinding and lapping work. Synthetic grit gave industry a supply that did not depend on mined diamonds. The report shares both the process and the apparatus behind it.
nasa-tm-19710016472-multicolor-photometr:
Thomas Kelsall of the Goddard Space Flight Center completed this work as a 1971 doctoral thesis at the University of Maryland. His adviser was astronomy professor Roger A Bell. Kelsall measured the light of supergiant stars and Cepheid variables through seven color filters. Cepheids pulse in brightness and serve as distance markers in astronomy. Careful color readings reveal their heat and makeup.

Kelsall combined the color readings into new indices. Those indices were built to cancel the reddening caused by dust between the stars. Four such cleaned indices came out of the work. Freed from dust effects, the colors speak more directly about the stars themselves. The thesis prints the full photometry results for both star groups.
nasa-tm-19710018186-estimation-of-shock-:
George E Kaattari of the Ames Research Center wrote this May 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,031. It gives quick methods for estimating the shock layer around a delta wing body space shuttle orbiter. At hypersonic speed, a shock wave wraps the craft in a thin hot layer. Designers need its thickness and the pressure it presses onto the skin.

Kaattari's methods compute the shock tilt angle along the body's center plane. They also give the surface pressure value for bodies held at an angle of attack. The methods suit shapes with oval cross sections. They also suit oblong sections with rounded corners. The usable angle range widens as the body grows more slender.
nasa-tm-19710025818-outgassing-tests-on-:
Lenora B Wells and David C Grana of the Langley Research Center ran these outgassing tests in September 1971, as NASA TM X-2360. They placed a microwave oven and freeze dried foods inside a vacuum chamber. The chamber pressure matched a possible spacecraft cabin level. In a closed cabin, gases leaking from gear and food build up fast. The team needed to know what the oven and meals would release.

The oven gave off mainly two butanol forms and hexane. Most foods released too little gas to identify clearly. Only the chicken chunks produced enough vapor for a firm reading. Their products were hexanal and methyl formate. Such checks helped judge everyday gear for crewed cabins.
nasa-tm-19720017059-a-procedure-for-pred:
Robert N Hosier of the Army Air Mobility laboratory and William H Mayes of the Langley Research Center wrote this noise procedure in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2556. Large blowdown wind tunnels are deafening while they run. Their roar fills the test section and spills over nearby communities. Designers needed a way to predict that noise before building. The procedure covers both the inside and outside fields.

Formulas predict the test section noise level and its spectrum. Two sources are treated, the tunnel burner and the turbulent boundary layer. Outside levels matter for workers and neighbors near the tunnel. The method gives overall levels, not just single tones. Tunnel planners could then add silencing where the numbers demanded. The work joined two Langley based research groups.
nasa-tm-19720017532-pre-emphasis-determi:
G R Wallace of the Marshall Space Flight Center and W E Salter of Sperry Rand Corporation issued these schedules on March 10, 1972, as NASA TM X-64648. Wallace worked in the Astrionics Laboratory. Their subject is pre-emphasis for a telemetry station. Pre-emphasis boosts weak high signals before sending, then trims them on receipt. Done right, it evens out noise across all channels. The station used FM subcarriers on an S-band link.

Eleven fixed bandwidth subcarriers shared the transmitter. The team computed schedules for three receiver signal strengths. Those strengths ranged from weak to comfortably strong. The goal was matching performance at the receiver's middle frequencies. Ground stations for spacecraft telemetry used such schedules daily. The report fixed values engineers could apply directly.
nasa-tm-19720020266-apollo-saturn-c00-00:
Kennedy Space Center issued this technical manual for the Apollo Saturn program. It gives operating and maintenance instructions for one ground system. The system protects communication cables from rusting away underground. Launch complex cables lie buried in soil or sunk in water. Florida's wet, salty ground attacks them constantly. Cathodic protection fights that corrosion with electric current. The manual belongs to the Apollo Saturn operations series.

The method impresses enough direct current onto the cables. That current stops or arrests the corrosion process. Crews maintaining the launch complex worked from these instructions. The system guarded cables at the Cape Kennedy launch area. Reliable communications were essential on launch day. Quiet manuals like this one kept the ground infrastructure alive between missions.
nasa-tm-19720024297-oxygen-hydrogen-inje:
John P. Wanhainen of the Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum in September 1972. Lewis, in Cleveland, Ohio, studied engines and power for flight. Wanhainen tested an injector, the part that feeds fuel into a rocket chamber. His fuel pair was liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.

The tests aimed at a strong, high thrust injector built from tubes set one inside another. He also checked how well the design worked with ablative chambers. Those chambers shed heat by slowly wearing away inside. Results like these helped engineers design rocket parts that could stand great heat and force.
nasa-tm-19720024581-flat-conductor-cable:
W. Angele wrote this NASA memorandum in August 1972 at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. He worked in the Process Engineering Laboratory there. His subject was flat conductor cable, a ribbon like form of wiring, and the connectors that join it.

Angele describes a connector series whose contacts are each sealed on their own. He covers how the design grew, what it had to meet, and how it was tested. He also deals with cost. Sealed contacts matter where moisture or dirt could spoil an electrical link. The report gave space hardware builders a tested option for compact wiring.
nets-to-catch-the-wind:
Elinor Wylie filled Nets to Catch the Wind with short poems, listed on its contents page one by one. Early titles include Beauty, The Eagle and the Mole, and Madman's Song. August, The Crooked Stick, and Wild Peaches follow. No prose frame joins them in the sample.

Later poems turn to a crowded trolley car, bells in the rain, and winter sleep. Village Mystery, Sunset on the Spire, and Escape keep the mix of town and nature scenes. Fire and Sleet and Candlelight and Blood Feud close the list given here. The titles alone show Wylie's range: bright images, sharp moods, and songs that catch at passing things.
old-mother-west-wind:
Thornton Burgess wrote these animal tales for young children. He dedicated the book to his mother and son. His son's love of stories inspired the tales, he says. The contents list sixteen chapters set in the Green Meadows. Old Mother West Wind sends her Merry Breezes out daily.

Stories explain why Grandfather Frog has no tail. Others tell why Jimmy Skunk wears stripes. Peter Rabbit, Reddy Fox, and Sammy Jay cause gentle trouble. Each tale teaches a small lesson about nature. Its meadow world began Burgess's long Bedtime Story series.
ormond: Ormond, Maria Edgeworth's Irish novel. The hero's tale. This book preserves that story. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
osceola-the-seminole-or-the-red-fawn-of-: Osceola the Seminole, or The Red Fawn of the Flower Land, by Mayne Reid. The Seminole chief. This book preserves that western. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
otto-of-the-silver-hand: Howard Pyle's 1888 Otto of the Silver Hand: a boy's medieval adventures. The great illustrator's classic, beautifully told. The children's Middle Ages. Pyle's Middle Ages for young readers, illustrated by the master himself, a classic for young readers.
our-mutual-friend: Dickens's last completed novel, a dark, brilliant story built around the London dust heaps where fortunes were made from rubbish. A drowned man, a will, mistaken identities, and the love of Lizzie Hexam weave through a portrait of a money-mad society. Complex and rewarding, it is Dickens's final masterpiece.
penguin-island: Anatole France's 1908 satire: penguins mistaken for humans are baptized, founding a civilization that mirrors France. Ironic, elegant, and devastating, it mocks history, religion, and politics. The great French satire of the modern age. France's irony has never been more elegant or more deadly.
ptolemy-tetrabiblos-ashmand:
Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, written around 150 CE, is astrology's foundational ancient textbook. J. M. Ashmand's 1822 translation is the classic English version preserved here. Ptolemy was also the greatest astronomer of the ancient world.

Four books lay out planets, signs, aspects, and their supposed influences. Weather, nations, births, and individual fortunes all fall under the system. Ptolemy presents astrology as a physical science of heavenly effects. His authority kept the system dominant for well over a thousand years. Ashmand's translation served generations of English readers and astrologers. The Tetrabiblos also witnesses Hellenistic star science from its most systematic mind. Few books of its kind have been read so long by so many.
ramsey-milholland: Tarkington follows Ramsey Milholland from boyhood scrapes to manhood in a small Indiana town. Funny and true, it smells of grass and summer evenings. The most American of coming-of-age tales, the most American of boyhood tales.
religio-medici-hydriotaphia-and-the-lett: Three meditations by Sir Thomas Browne, the 17th-century physician and philosopher. Religio Medici is his personal confession of faith, Hydriotaphia (Urn Burial) his famous reflection on death inspired by ancient burial urns, and the Letter a tender farewell to a dying friend. Browne's rich, musical prose made him one of the glories of English literature, beloved by readers from Coleridge to Borges.
saint-george-for-england: Saint George for England, G. A. Henty's Crecy and Poitiers tale. The saint's England. This book preserves that historical novel. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
sganarelle-or-the-self-deceived-husband: Molière's brisk one-act comedy turns on Sganarelle, a husband convinced his wife is unfaithful — and wrong about nearly everything. Mistaken identities and quick misunderstandings drive the farce at a breathless pace. An early triumph of the young Molière, it shows his comic machinery already running at full speed.
sima-qian-memoires-historiques-chavannes:
Édouard Chavannes printed the second tome of his French Shiji in 1896, holding chapters five through twelve. Sima Qian wrote the work around 91 BCE. These chapters tell how the feudal world of Zhou gave way to one empire, then to the Han house.

Qin unites China, the First Emperor rules and falls, and Xiang Yu fights Liu Bang for the throne. The annals end with Gaozu, the peasant who founded Han. Chavannes notes each hard name and rite with care. The tome covers the most dramatic turn in early Chinese history, in the words of its greatest historian.
